title: Lava dropped into a pond: what the plume is made of
question: Which one reads as a steam plume rather than something bouncing up and down?
context_md:
Your report: lava into water "rises about 5 ft in the air and then drops back into rain... it almost looks like bouncing because it goes up and down so fast."

New scene `filmstrip scene=lavadrop` — an 800-cell lava blob released over the middle of a 199-wide pond, which is your report literally. Read left to right, top row then bottom row: frames 40, 100, 160, 220 / 280, 340, 400, 460.

What I measured, and it was not rate or height: the plume held **421 water cells standing in the air** at peak, spread through its whole 40-row height rather than pooled at the top. Those are condensate falling back *through* the steam still rising — and a falling liquid displaces a gas, so each droplet shoves steam cells downward as it goes. That is the bouncing itself, which is why it reads as the steam going up and down when a gas has no downward move at all.

The change: steam condensing **with open sky above it** hands its water to the atmospheric bank instead of leaving a cell. Sealed pockets and roofed chambers are untouched. Conservation holds to 0.1 of a cell-equivalent.

**What I am unsure of and want your eye on:** the plume still tops out ~30-40 rows and then stops at 45C rather than fading. You said to look at height in the app yourself — this is the artifact to look at it on.
